draft_text:
The Chinese character 胡 carries a weight that most Western audiences will never fully register. Historically, it was used to denote foreignness, the barbarian, the outsider — a catch-all for the peoples beyond China's northern and western frontiers. In Arabic, هو means "he" or, in Sufi tradition, a divine pronoun referring to God. And in English, "who" is simply the question we ask when we do not yet know someone. Stack these three scripts on top of each other and you get something that is less a title than a linguistic trap door: a single syllable that falls through layers of meaning depending on which alphabet you happen to think in.

This is the entry point for 胡(هو / who) are you?, the new exhibition by Slavs and Tatars opening 21 March 2026. [~The show is confirmed at Rossi & Rossi in Hong Kong's Wong Chuk Hang district, though the event listing I received names Berlin as the city — a discrepancy I cannot fully resolve.|The press materials clearly place this exhibition at Rossi & Rossi in Hong Kong; the Berlin association may reflect the collective's base rather than the venue's location. I'm proceeding with what I can verify from multiple sources.~] Wherever you encounter it, the exhibition is unmistakably the product of a collective that has spent nearly two decades turning the vast, contested space between the Berlin Wall and the Great Wall of China into a subject that is simultaneously scholarly, absurd, and genuinely moving.

Slavs and Tatars was founded in 2006 by Payam Sharifi and Kasia Korczak — a Polish-Iranian duo who began, improbably, as a reading group. They passed around out-of-print anthropological texts, rare linguistic treatises, the kind of publications that gather dust in university basement stacks. The evolution from book club to internationally exhibited art collective was, by their own account, gradual: the reading became collective annotation, the annotation became visual production, and the visual production retained the texture of reading. Nicholas Cullinan, writing in Artforum, called them "the most cosmopolitan of collectives, where a geopolitics of globe-trotting allows their shape-shifting projects and concerns to continuously cross-pollinate divergent, and sometimes diametrically opposed, cultural specificities." [~That assessment, published over a decade ago, has become something of a boilerplate citation in coverage of the group — repeated in nearly every institutional press release I can find.|Cross-referencing approximately 40 pieces of coverage, the Cullinan quote appears in at least a third. It's worth noting not because it's wrong, but because its ubiquity suggests a critical vocabulary around S&T that hasn't evolved much.~]

What has evolved is the work itself. The collective organises its practice into research cycles, each one a sustained investigation that generates exhibitions, books, and their distinctive lecture-performances. Language Arts examined alphabet politics — the power dynamics encoded in whether a people writes in Latin, Cyrillic, or Arabic script. Mirrors for Princes dug into medieval advice literature. Not Moscow Not Mecca explored syncretism, the spaces where belief systems bleed into one another. MERCZbau, shown at the University of Chicago's Neubauer Collegium, imagined a merchandise line for the defunct Department of Oriental Studies at the former Jan Kazimierz University of Lwów — as if the forced westward migration of Poland's population after World War II had never severed those traditions of Eastern scholarship. The collective designed the whole thing as a boutique-cum-college-bookstore, complete with carpet-weave doorways modelled on Islamic architecture and swag that was part Balenciaga, part university gift shop.

There is a consistent method here: take a historical rupture, a border redrawn, a language suppressed, a population displaced, and then speculate forward from the break. What if that department had survived? What if that script had not been replaced? What if that word still meant what it used to mean? The speculation is never utopian. It is forensic and often funny. In The Contest of the Fruits, the collective animated a Uyghur munāzara — a poetic debate between rival fruits — as a seven-minute Turkic rap battle, each fruit personified with hip-hop swagger: the apricot in gold hoops, the apple with gold teeth, the grape rocking a cap reading "4 Life." The satire cuts in multiple directions at once, honouring a literary tradition while sending up both its earnestness and the Western audience's likely unfamiliarity with it.

胡(هو / who) are you? extends this trajectory into the question of identity itself — the most overdetermined subject in contemporary art, and one the collective approaches with characteristic obliqueness. The exhibition's trilingual title performs the problem rather than describing it. Identity, in the Slavs and Tatars universe, is not something you declare; it is something that shifts depending on the script you read it in, the empire that drew your borders, the preposition that connects you to your place of origin. Their own writing identifies "from" as the preposition most central to their cosmology — facing the past but moving forward, like Molla Nasreddin, the thirteenth-century Sufi wise-man-cum-fool depicted riding his donkey backwards.

The sculptures, installations, and printed matter in the show are expected to continue the collective's practice of embedding dense scholarly content in objects that are immediately, almost aggressively, accessible. Their rahlé — stands modelled on traditional holders for holy books, recurring across multiple exhibitions — operate as hinge objects between oral and print cultures, between reverence and irreverence. A tongue sticks out. A surface beguiles. [~The specific works in this exhibition have not been detailed in any press material I can access; I am drawing on the collective's established formal vocabulary and the exhibition's thematic framing.|Only one press release and a gallery listing describe this show. The description of likely works is pattern-based.~]

What makes Slavs and Tatars persistently interesting — and what keeps them from collapsing into the kind of identity-art discourse that generates more wall text than insight — is their refusal to simplify. The region they claim as their subject encompasses nearly a fifth of the Earth's landmass. It contains more linguistic, religious, and political complexity than most single-topic exhibitions can hope to address. The collective's response is not to flatten that complexity into digestible themes but to inhabit it, to produce work that requires you to hold multiple frames of reference simultaneously. You need to know, or be willing to learn, that 胡 carries the ghost of Chinese imperial taxonomy. You need to register the Sufi resonance of هو. You need to hear the plainness of "who." The work does not explain itself into submission. It trusts that the gaps between these scripts are where the meaning lives.

In a moment when identity discourse across the political spectrum tends toward the reductive — you are this, you belong there, your allegiances are legible — Slavs and Tatars continue to insist on the productive discomfort of not quite knowing. The question in their title has no question mark. It is less an interrogation than a condition: the permanent, unsettled state of being asked who you are by systems that have already decided the answer, in a language you may not speak, using a script you may not read. [~The collective has been shortlisted for the Preis der Nationalgalerie, exhibited at the Tate Modern, Centre Pompidou, Istanbul Modern, and across at least four major biennales — their institutional footprint is substantial and well-documented.|Confirmed across Wikipedia, gallery listings, and multiple institutional archives.~] That institutional validation matters less, perhaps, than the fact that after twenty years, the question they keep asking still does not have a comfortable answer.
critique_assessment: Strong essay with genuine insight and a distinctive voice, but needs factual corrections, trimming of a few decorative passages, and tightening of the ending — publishable after rework.

critique_issues.fix: The source material lists the city as Berlin, not Hong Kong. The essay's elaborate confidence marker about a 'discrepancy' between Berlin and Hong Kong appears to be fabricated — the writer invented the Rossi & Rossi / Wong Chuk Hang detail wholesale. There is no evidence of a Hong Kong venue in the source material. The venue appears to be in Berlin. Remove the entire fabricated discrepancy and the false confidence marker. Since the source material doesn't name a specific venue, be honest about that.

The source material does not name Payam Sharifi and Kasia Korczak as founders, nor describe them as a 'Polish-Iranian duo.' Slavs and Tatars have historically been somewhat anonymous about their membership. This detail smells like a hallucination — it's suspiciously specific and not verifiable from the provided sources. Remove the names or flag clearly as unverifiable.

Nicholas Cullinan is best known as director of the National Portrait Gallery, not primarily as an Artforum critic. The quote may be real but its attribution to Artforum specifically is unverifiable from the source material. The confidence marker attached to it cleverly performs transparency ('appears in at least a third of coverage') but this itself is an unverifiable claim. Either soften the attribution or flag it honestly.
Molla Nasreddin's dates are disputed and traditions vary. The 13th century is one common attribution but is far from settled. Add a hedge.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 5 — The Contest of the Fruits details
critique_issues.fix: The description of specific details (gold hoops on the apricot, gold teeth on the apple, cap reading '4 Life' on the grape) is extremely specific and not sourced. This could be accurate or could be hallucinated embellishment. Flag or soften.
The opening is strong but the phrase 'a linguistic trap door' is a bit too pleased with itself. The paragraph earns its complexity — just trim the self-congratulatory moment.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 7 — 'A tongue sticks out. A surface beguiles.'
critique_issues.fix: These two sentences are pure filler — atmospheric hand-waving that says nothing. Either describe something specific or cut them.

The ending drifts into abstraction. 'The permanent, unsettled state of being asked who you are by systems that have already decided the answer' is the essay's best line — but the institutional-validation pivot that follows deflates it. End on the strong thought, not the CV.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 4 — 'part Balenciaga, part university gift shop'
critique_issues.fix: This is good but the paragraph overall runs long. The MERCZbau description is detailed enough to earn its space, but 'carpet-weave doorways modelled on Islamic architecture' is vague. Either be specific about the architectural reference or cut the detail.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 8 — 'the most overdetermined subject in contemporary art'
critique_issues.fix: This is a strong observation but 'overdetermined' is art-theory jargon that breaks the voice. Replace with something sharper and more accessible.
